topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A retry or cache policy often depends on time and external results. Waiting for real minutes or relying on an unreliable service makes unit tests slow and nondeterministic. Harbor’s short-lived cache accepts a clock and a source explicitly so tests can advance time and control failures without disguising those doubles as real infrastructure.

topics.summary: A stub returns configured answers, a fake supplies a simplified working implementation, and a mock commonly verifies expected interactions. topics.title: 8.1.2 Controlling Test Inputs
topics.summary: Make time, randomness, and external responses explicit inputs at the boundary where they affect decisions. A deterministic test can arrange a hit, expiration, or source failure precisely. Hidden calls to a global clock make such cases harder to reproduce and tempt tests to use fragile sleep intervals.

topics.title: 8.2.1 Injecting Dependencies
topics.summary: Dependency injection means supplying a dependency rather than constructing or locating it secretly inside the component. Constructor references, callable objects, templates, or an explicit context can all implement it. A virtual interface is useful when runtime substitution is needed, but it is not mandatory for every small function.

topics.title: Trace the implementation

blocks.text: The refresh computes a candidate before committing cache state. If the source throws, the old value and timestamp remain intact, but get propagates the failure rather than silently returning stale data. That is one policy choice; a stale-on-error policy would need a different contract and tests. A backward clock value forces refresh rather than subtracting into a misleading negative age.

The source call count is asserted because avoiding unnecessary refreshes is part of this cache’s behavior, not merely an incidental implementation detail.
